request: Draw a demand and supply diagram, then show demand increasing.

commands.speak: What happens to price and quantity when more people want something — ice cream on the first hot day, say?
Demand: the lower the price, the more ice cream people want.
Supply: the higher the price, the more sellers are willing to make and sell.
On an ordinary day they meet here: the one price at which buyers want exactly what sellers offer.
Then the heat arrives. At every price, people now want more: the whole demand curve moves right.
At the old price, the queue is longer than what sellers have.
So the price climbs — some buyers give up, sellers make more — until the two meet again: higher price, more ice cream.
And supply never moved. Sellers slid along their own curve: a change in the quantity supplied, not in supply.

quiz.question: If supply had shifted right instead, what would the price do?
quiz.right: It falls: more is offered at every price, so sellers must cut the price to find buyers.

request: Draw a decision tree for choosing between surgery and watchful waiting, with QALY payoffs.

commands.speak: Should she have surgery now, or wait and watch? A decision tree is one way to answer that: it lays out each choice, the chances of what follows, and what each outcome is worth — then weighs them.
This square is the decision we control. Surgery leads to a circle — a chance node — because its outcome is uncertain.
With probability 0.85 the operation succeeds; with 0.15 there is a complication.
Each ending is worth something: 9.2 QALYs after recovery, 5.1 after a complication.
Watchful waiting has no chance node here: 7.4 QALYs, for sure.
To compare a sure 7.4 with a gamble, weigh each outcome by its chance: the expected value.
Success: 0.85 times 9.2…
…plus complication: 0.15 times 5.1.
That is 7.82 plus 0.77: about 8.6 QALYs expected from surgery.
And waiting: 7.4.
8.6 beats 7.4, so the tree says operate: we cut the branch with the lower expected value.
That is how a tree decides: average at each chance node, then take the best branch. The sum can move aside.
But the tree shows the trade-off; it does not make it. A patient who fears that complication more than the numbers say may still wait, and the tree shows what she gives up.
Why is the first square of chocolate so much better than the fourth? Economists call it diminishing marginal utility.
Here is how much you enjoy eating squares one after another, added up.
The first square takes you from nothing to thirty-six.
The second adds twenty-three: still good, but two squares do not make you twice as happy.
The third adds fifteen, the fourth only nine: each extra square — the marginal one — adds less.
Why? The craving gets used up. The first square meets a real hunger for sweetness; by the fourth you are close to full.
It is not a law of nature, though. A new song can be better the fourth time than the first, because you hear more in it each time.
Its curve bends UP before it flattens: rising marginal utility, for a while, and then even the best song wears out.
And timing matters: the rule is about units in a row. Next week, a square is as good as the first one was today.
That is why one more of something you already have plenty of is worth so little to you — and why you would pay less for it.

request: Show a client sending a request to a server that queries a database.

commands.speak: What happens between clicking “my profile” and seeing it? Three parts take turns: your browser, a server, and its database.
The browser asks the server for the profile page.
The server does not have your profile to hand. It asks the database for exactly one row: yours.
The database sends that row back.
And the server fills it into a page and returns it to the browser.
Round trip: out and back, twice, usually in a fraction of a second.
Why not let the browser ask the database itself? Because the server is where the rules live: it checks who you are and asks only for what you may see.

request: How does a bicycle pump push air into a tyre?

commands.speak: A pump pushes air into a tyre already tighter than the air outside. Why does none of it come back?
The piston seals the tube, trapping a column of ordinary air beneath it.
Push down, and that air is squeezed into half the space, so its pressure climbs past the tyre's.
At the end of the hose sits a flap that only the higher pressure can push open.
Let go, and the tyre's own pressure slams it shut. Each stroke adds air and none returns: the pump never holds the pressure — the valve does.

request: Why does a dropped ball speed up? Show the equations with the curve.

spec.title: Why a falling ball stops speeding up

elements.details: With air resistance growing as $kv^2$, the speed is $$v(t) = v_t \tanh(g t / v_t)$$ close to $g t$ at first, and closing in on $v_t$ ever more slowly.
At terminal speed the ball stops accelerating, $a = 0$, so $mg = k v_t^2$ and $$v_t = \sqrt{mg/k}$$ A heavier ball of the same size falls faster; a feather’s $v_t$ is well under 1 m/s.
Newton’s second law for the falling ball: $$m\,a = mg - k v^2$$ where $k$ depends on the ball’s size and shape and on the air’s density.

card.title: Why a falling ball stops speeding up

commands.speak: Why does a falling ball stop speeding up? Drop two balls from a tall tower: one with no air around it at all, one through ordinary air.
At first they fall side by side. Then the one in air falls behind.
Here is where each ball was, once every second. With no air, every second’s gap is longer than the last: it never stops speeding up.
In air, the gaps grow at first — and then stop growing. That ball has stopped speeding up.
The same two falls, as speed against time.
No air: gravity adds 9.8 metres per second, every second — a straight line.
In air: the same start, then a curve that levels off.
The reason is a second force. The net pull is gravity, m g, minus the push of the air — and that push grows with the speed squared.
So the faster the ball goes, the less pull is left over to speed it up.
At about 42 metres per second — 150 kilometres an hour — the air pushes up as hard as gravity pulls down. No net force, no more speeding up: terminal speed.
That is the even spacing in the flashes: the same distance every second.

quiz.question: A feather and a baseball are dropped together. Why does the feather lag?
choices: Gravity pulls it less per kilo
The air stops it speeding up much sooner
quiz.right: Gravity adds the same 9.8 m/s each second to both; the feather’s air resistance matches its tiny weight almost at once.

request: What does a wind turbine's gearbox actually do?

commands.speak: Why does a wind turbine carry a gearbox up there? Because its two ends want very different speeds.
Each blade is longer than an airliner’s wing.
Wind pushes on the blades…
…and the rotor turns — slowly. About fifteen times a minute.
It has to be slow: the tips of blades this long already cut the air at nearly 300 kilometres an hour, and faster means noise and worn-away edges.
At the other end sits the generator. It makes electricity by sweeping magnets past coils of wire, and it wants about fifteen hundred turns a minute to do that well.
In between: a big gear on the slow shaft from the rotor…
…driving a small one. Each turn of the big wheel spins the small one many times: speed up, force down.
Three such steps in a row multiply fifteen turns a minute into fifteen hundred.
The catch: the gearbox is what breaks most often, a hundred metres up. So many new turbines drop it, and use a huge generator with so many magnets that it works at fifteen turns a minute.

request: Explain with a dialogue whether capping rents is a good idea #qa

commands.speak: Rents in this city are sky-high. Wouldn't a legal maximum rent help?
Let's look. Demand: the lower the rent, the more people want a flat of their own.
Supply: the higher the rent, the more flats landlords offer.
Left alone, the rent settles where the two meet.
Now the cap: no rent above this line.
So everyone pays less?
At the capped rent, this many people want a flat…
…but landlords offer only this many.
The gap is the shortage: more people want a flat than there are flats to rent.
But whoever does get one pays less?
Yes — for them the cap works. The cost falls on the ones in the gap, left without a flat, and on the landlords.
And the size of that gap depends on time. Next year, the buildings are still there…
…so supply hardly moves, few flats disappear, and the cap mostly moves money from landlords to tenants.
Ten years on, it's different.
Building flats to rent pays less, old ones get less upkeep or are sold off, and the shortage grows.
So the real problem was never the rent itself?
It's too few flats. A cap shares out the flats there are; only more flats make room for everyone.

quiz.question: Over many years, what does a rent cap do to the number of flats for rent?
quiz.right: It lowers it: at a capped rent, building and keeping up flats to rent pays less.

request: Roll a die 100 times and then 10,000 times and show how the shares of each face settle down

elements.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
def shares(n):
    rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, size=n)
    return [round(float((rolls == f).mean()), 3) for f in range(1, 7)]
frames = [shares(n) for n in (10, 100, 1000, 10000)]

commands.speak: How many rolls does it take to see that a die is fair? If it is, each face comes up one time in six in the long run: this line.
Ten rolls: not a single three, and three sixes. Is the die loaded?
A hundred rolls: every face turns up now, but the shares still run from 13 to 21 percent.
A thousand: between 15 and 18 percent.
Ten thousand: all six within a point or so of the line.
Why does it settle? Not because luck evens out. After ten thousand rolls, the count of sixes is typically off by about forty — more than after a hundred, where it is off by about four.
But four out of a hundred is four percent, and forty out of ten thousand is under half a percent. The misses grow with the square root of the rolls; the rolls themselves grow faster.
That is the law of large numbers: early luck is never paid back — it is diluted.

quiz.question: Ten rolls, and no three yet. The chance the next roll is a three is…
quiz.right: One in six: the die has no memory. Old luck is diluted by new rolls, never paid back.

request: In R, show a tidyverse pipeline summarising a small table by group.

elements.code:
library(dplyr)
scores <- tibble(class = c("a", "a", "b", "b", "c"), score = c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10))
scores |>
  group_by(class) |>
  summarise(mean_score = mean(score), pupils = n())

commands.speak: How do you get the average for each group in a table, in R? First a helper: R has few commands for tables built in, and library(dplyr) loads a package that adds them.
Then a small table to work on — five pupils, their class, and a score. The arrow stores it under the name scores; tibble is dplyr’s word for a table.
Now the recipe. scores, then this sign, the pipe: take what is on the left and hand it to the next step.
group_by sorts the rows into one pile per class.
And summarise boils each pile down to one row: the mean score, and n, how many pupils were in the pile.
The result: one row per class. Class a averages three, b seven — and c is ten, but from a single pupil, which is why the count is worth keeping.

request: Show what happens to the shares of dice faces when you roll a hundred times, then ten thousand — in pure Python.

elements.code:
import random
random.seed(7)
def shares(n):
    rolls = [random.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(n)]
    return [round(rolls.count(f) / n, 3) for f in range(1, 7)]
frames = [shares(100), shares(10000)]

commands.speak: Is a die fair? Ask it a hundred times, then ten thousand — in a Python that loads in a second. A hundred rolls: the faces come up unevenly.
Ten thousand rolls, and every face settles toward one sixth.
